_meta.title: Nehru-era policies that shaped the states (1947–1964)
_meta.purpose: Connect the primary-source memoirs (reading room) to how policy shaped India's states — each policy links to where it's discussed in the book and to the states on the map. Impact is stated sourced-or-a-gap; this is NOT a causal claim that a policy alone caused an outcome.
_meta.sources: Wikipedia (per-policy articles) + standard histories; dates/structure are citable facts, 'impact' notes are directional and marked where they are a gap.
_meta.honesty: History is contested. These cards say what a policy DID (documented) and which states it touched — not that it single-handedly 'caused' a state's condition today. Causation needs analysis; gaps are marked.

policies.title: States Reorganisation Act, 1956
policies.what: Redrew India's internal map along LINGUISTIC lines — the largest boundary change since independence. Replaced the Part A/B/C/D system with 14 states + 6 union territories (Fazl Ali Commission, 1953–55).
policies.shaped_note: Formed/redrew nearly every state — Andhra Pradesh (Telugu), Kerala (Malayalam), Mysore→Karnataka (Kannada), Bombay→later Maharashtra/Gujarat (Marathi/Gujarati).
policies.impact: The state boundaries the atlas maps today largely date from here. It set the precedent that language = state — the organising logic of Indian federalism.
policies.impact_gap: Whether linguistic states helped or hurt development is a live scholarly debate — not settled, so not asserted.

policies.title: Planning Commission & the Five-Year Plans
policies.what: Set up central economic planning: the Planning Commission allocated capital to states by plan. The 2nd Plan (Mahalanobis) bet on heavy industry and public-sector steel.
policies.shaped_note: Directed where public capital and heavy industry landed — the mineral-belt states got the steel plants; others got dams and irrigation.
policies.impact: Central-to-state capital allocation as a system starts here — the ancestor of the Finance Commission devolution the atlas tracks.
policies.impact_gap: Per-state plan-outlay-to-outcome is not cleanly reconstructable from open data for the 1950s — a gap.

policies.title: Public-sector steel towns
policies.what: State-built integrated steel plants — Bhilai (Soviet aid), Rourkela (West German), Durgapur (British) — planted heavy industry and whole new cities in the mineral belt.
policies.shaped_note: Bhilai (then MP, now Chhattisgarh), Rourkela (Odisha), Durgapur (West Bengal) — company towns that reshaped their districts.
policies.impact: Created industrial districts and PSU employment that still anchor these local economies.
policies.impact_gap: The long-run local prosperity vs displacement balance is contested — stated as documented facts, not a verdict.

policies.title: The IITs & scientific institutions
policies.what: Founded the Indian Institutes of Technology and a network of national labs — Nehru's bet on science and higher technical education as nation-building.
policies.shaped_note: IIT Kharagpur (1951), then Bombay, Madras, Kanpur, Delhi — concentrated elite technical capacity in these states.
policies.impact: Seeded the human-capital clusters that later feed India's tech economy — a state-level advantage that compounds.
policies.impact_gap: Attributing a state's present tech economy to a 1950s institute is exactly the causal leap we DON'T make — a gap.

policies.title: Bhakra-Nangal & the big dams
policies.what: Multipurpose river-valley projects — Nehru's “temples of modern India.” Bhakra-Nangal on the Sutlej brought irrigation and power to the northwest.
policies.shaped_note: Bhakra-Nangal irrigated Punjab/Haryana/Rajasthan — the water base later crucial to the Green Revolution.
policies.impact: The irrigation these dams provided underpins the agricultural map the atlas shows in the northwest.
policies.impact_gap: Dam displacement and long-run ecological cost are real and debated — not netted out here.
